claim: 78% (171/218) of Pvalb mRNA-containing neurons with cell bodies in and around stratum pyramidale contain both Oprm1 and Oprd1 mRNA
source: We first confirmed that both MORs and DORs are co-expressed in PV-BCs using fluorescence in situ hybridization, which revealed that 78% (171/218) of Pvalb mRNA-containing neurons with cell bodies in and around stratum pyramidale contain both Oprm1 and Oprd1 mRNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence in situ hybridization data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B, showing quantification of mRNA co-localization.

claim: Bath perfusion of DAMGO (1 μM) strongly reduced the optically evoked IPSC
source: Bath perfusion of either DAMGO (1 μM) or SNC162 (1 μM) strongly reduced the optically evoked IPSC (oIPSC) to a similar degree (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing oIPSC suppression in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Bath perfusion of SNC162 (1 μM) strongly reduced the optically evoked IPSC
source: Bath perfusion of either DAMGO (1 μM) or SNC162 (1 μM) strongly reduced the optically evoked IPSC (oIPSC) to a similar degree (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing oIPSC suppression in Figure 1B-D.

claim: DAMGO and SNC162 reduced oIPSC to a similar degree
source: Bath perfusion of either DAMGO (1 μM) or SNC162 (1 μM) strongly reduced the optically evoked IPSC (oIPSC) to a similar degree (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of oIPSC suppression by DAMGO and SNC162 shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Sequential application of DAMGO and SNC162 only slightly increased the degree of suppression compared to either drug alone (DAMGO: 0.69 ± 0.05, n = 9 cells; SNC162: 0.70 ± 0.05, n = 9 cells; both: 0.76 ± 0.03, n = 18 cells; no significant differences)
source: Sequential drug application only slightly increased the degree of suppression compared to either drug alone (DAMGO: 0.69 ± 0.05, n = 9 cells; SNC162: 0.70 ± 0.05, n = 9 cells; both: 0.76 ± 0.03, n = 18 cells; no significant differences, ordinary one-way ANOVA) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of oIPSC suppression with statistical analysis showing no significant differences.

claim: Application of pairs of optical stimuli revealed small increases in the paired-pulse ratio in the presence of DAMGO (BL: 0.47 ± 0.08; DAMGO: 0.68 ± 0.14; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.0078)
source: In both cases, application of pairs of optical stimuli (50 ms apart) revealed small increases in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in the presence of the opioid agonist, consistent with a presynaptic mechanism of action for the opioid receptor (BL: 0.47 ± 0.08; DAMGO: 0.68 ± 0.14; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.0078, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; BL: 0.42 ± 0.05; SNC162: 0.56 ± 0.07; n = 8 pairs; p = 0.016, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Application of pairs of optical stimuli revealed small increases in the paired-pulse ratio in the presence of SNC162 (BL: 0.42 ± 0.05; SNC162: 0.56 ± 0.07; n = 8 pairs; p = 0.016)
source: In both cases, application of pairs of optical stimuli (50 ms apart) revealed small increases in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in the presence of the opioid agonist, consistent with a presynaptic mechanism of action for the opioid receptor (BL: 0.47 ± 0.08; DAMGO: 0.68 ± 0.14; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.0078, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; BL: 0.42 ± 0.05; SNC162: 0.56 ± 0.07; n = 8 pairs; p = 0.016, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: Increases in paired-pulse ratio are consistent with a presynaptic mechanism of action for the opioid receptor
source: In both cases, application of pairs of optical stimuli (50 ms apart) revealed small increases in the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) in the presence of the opioid agonist, consistent with a presynaptic mechanism of action for the opioid receptor (BL: 0.47 ± 0.08; DAMGO: 0.68 ± 0.14; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.0078, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; BL: 0.42 ± 0.05; SNC162: 0.56 ± 0.07; n = 8 pairs; p = 0.016, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge that increases in paired-pulse ratio indicate presynaptic mechanisms.

claim: DAMGO showed greater desensitization than SNC162 with sustained application (DAMGOearly: 0.69 ± 0.05; DAMGOlate: 0.44 ± 0.07; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.0038; SNC162early: 0.70 ± 0.05; SNC162late: 0.61 ± 0.06; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.048)
source: With sustained application, both the effects of DAMGO and SNC162 appeared to desensitize slightly, with DAMGO showing greater desensitization (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H, I) (DAMGOearly: 0.69 ± 0.05; DAMGOlate: 0.44 ± 0.07; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.0038, paired t-test; SNC162early: 0.70 ± 0.05; SNC162late: 0.61 ± 0.06; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.048, paired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing early and late phases of drug application with statistical testing.

claim: Both MORs and DORs suppress the output of PV-BCs in a mutually occlusive manner
source: These results reveal that both MORs and DORs suppress the output of PV-BCs in a mutually occlusive manner.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing that sequential application of DAMGO and SNC162 produces only slightly more suppression than either drug alone.

claim: Bath application of WIN55,212 (1 μM) resulted in only modest eIPSC suppression (0.25 ± 0.07, n = 8 cells)
source: Consistent with only a minor contribution to the electrically evoked IPSC (eIPSC) from CB1R-expressing CCK-BCs, bath application of the CB1R agonist WIN55,212 (1 μM) resulted in only modest eIPSC suppression (0.25 ± 0.07, n = 8 cells), and application of WIN55,212 in the presence of DAMGO produced only slightly more suppression than DAMGO alone, although this effect was not significant, suggesting some occlusion (DAMGO: 0.67 ± 0.02, n = 12 cells; WIN55,212 + DAMGO: 0.79 ± 0.03, n = 8 cells; p = 0.14, ordinary one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparison test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of eIPSC suppression by WIN55,212.

claim: Application of WIN55,212 in the presence of DAMGO produced only slightly more suppression than DAMGO alone (DAMGO: 0.67 ± 0.02, n = 12 cells; WIN55,212 + DAMGO: 0.79 ± 0.03, n = 8 cells; p = 0.14)
source: Consistent with only a minor contribution to the electrically evoked IPSC (eIPSC) from CB1R-expressing CCK-BCs, bath application of the CB1R agonist WIN55,212 (1 μM) resulted in only modest eIPSC suppression (0.25 ± 0.07, n = 8 cells), and application of WIN55,212 in the presence of DAMGO produced only slightly more suppression than DAMGO alone, although this effect was not significant, suggesting some occlusion (DAMGO: 0.67 ± 0.02, n = 12 cells; WIN55,212 + DAMGO: 0.79 ± 0.03, n = 8 cells; p = 0.14, ordinary one-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparison test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing DAMGO alone to DAMGO plus WIN55,212 with statistical testing.

claim: DAMGO and SNC162 exhibited strong mutual occlusion of the eIPSC (DAMGO: 0.69 ± 0.02, n = 14 cells; SNC162: 0.63 ± 0.06, n = 9 cells; both: 0.75 ± 0.04, n = 14 cells; no significant differences)
source: As with optogenetic stimulation, DAMGO and SNC162 exhibited strong mutual occlusion of the eIPSC (DAMGO: 0.69 ± 0.02, n = 14 cells; SNC162: 0.63 ± 0.06, n = 9 cells; both: 0.75 ± 0.04, n = 14 cells; no significant differences, ordinary one-way ANOVA), and a small increase in PPR was produced by DAMGO but not SNC162 (BL: 0.67 ± 0.03; DAMGO: 0.80 ± 0.04; n = 11 pairs; p = 0.019, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; BL: 0.65 ± 0.02; SNC162: 0.77 ± 0.04; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.055, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 1F–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of eIPSC suppression with statistical analysis.

claim: A small increase in PPR was produced by DAMGO (BL: 0.67 ± 0.03; DAMGO: 0.80 ± 0.04; n = 11 pairs; p = 0.019)
source: As with optogenetic stimulation, DAMGO and SNC162 exhibited strong mutual occlusion of the eIPSC (DAMGO: 0.69 ± 0.02, n = 14 cells; SNC162: 0.63 ± 0.06, n = 9 cells; both: 0.75 ± 0.04, n = 14 cells; no significant differences, ordinary one-way ANOVA), and a small increase in PPR was produced by DAMGO but not SNC162 (BL: 0.67 ± 0.03; DAMGO: 0.80 ± 0.04; n = 11 pairs; p = 0.019, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; BL: 0.65 ± 0.02; SNC162: 0.77 ± 0.04; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.055, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 1F–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: SNC162 did not produce a significant increase in PPR (BL: 0.65 ± 0.02; SNC162: 0.77 ± 0.04; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.055)
source: As with optogenetic stimulation, DAMGO and SNC162 exhibited strong mutual occlusion of the eIPSC (DAMGO: 0.69 ± 0.02, n = 14 cells; SNC162: 0.63 ± 0.06, n = 9 cells; both: 0.75 ± 0.04, n = 14 cells; no significant differences, ordinary one-way ANOVA), and a small increase in PPR was produced by DAMGO but not SNC162 (BL: 0.67 ± 0.03; DAMGO: 0.80 ± 0.04; n = 11 pairs; p = 0.019, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test; BL: 0.65 ± 0.02; SNC162: 0.77 ± 0.04; n = 9 pairs; p = 0.055, Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed rank test) (Figure 1F–J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by paired-pulse ratio measurements with statistical testing showing lack of significance.

claim: LE exhibits approximately threefold greater potency for DORs than MORs in regulating perisomatic inhibition (EC50 values: ACSF 3.28 ± 0.47 mW, CTOP 2.29 ± 0.61 mW, TIPP-Psi 9.30 ± 1.40 mW)
source: The power-response curve revealed that LE exhibits approximately threefold greater potency for DORs than MORs in regulating perisomatic inhibition (EC50 values in the absence [black, 3.28 ± 0.47 mW] and presence of either CTOP [red, 2.29 ± 0.61 mW] or TIPP-Psi [blue, 9.30 ± 1.40 mW]).
evidence: The claim is supported by EC50 values derived from power-response curves showing approximately threefold difference.

claim: DOR activation largely accounts for the actions of LE in the absence of antagonists
source: Moreover, DOR activation largely accounts for the actions of LE in the absence of antagonists.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the power-response curves showing that the curve in ACSF closely matches the curve in CTOP (MOR blocked).

claim: DOR exhibited kinetics indistinct from the drug-free condition at 20 Hz (CTOP at 20 Hz, tau = 419 ± 105 ms, n = 11 cells; ACSF at 20 Hz, tau = 259 ± 30 ms, n = 8 cells)
source: At 20 Hz, DOR (CTOP at 20 Hz, tau = 419 ± 105 ms, n = 11 cells) exhibited kinetics indistinct from the drug-free condition (artificial cerebrospinal fluid [ACSF] at 20 Hz, tau = 259 ± 30 ms, n = 8 cells), but the time constant of MOR-mediated suppression was surprisingly slow (TIPP-Psi at 20 Hz, tau = 683 ± 36 ms, n = 6 cells; p = 0.0046, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by time constant measurements with statistical comparison.

claim: The time constant of MOR-mediated suppression was surprisingly slow at 20 Hz (TIPP-Psi at 20 Hz, tau = 683 ± 36 ms, n = 6 cells; p = 0.0046)
source: At 20 Hz, DOR (CTOP at 20 Hz, tau = 419 ± 105 ms, n = 11 cells) exhibited kinetics indistinct from the drug-free condition (artificial cerebrospinal fluid [ACSF] at 20 Hz, tau = 259 ± 30 ms, n = 8 cells), but the time constant of MOR-mediated suppression was surprisingly slow (TIPP-Psi at 20 Hz, tau = 683 ± 36 ms, n = 6 cells; p = 0.0046, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by time constant measurements with statistical significance testing.

claim: The extent of eIPSC suppression correlated inversely with the frequency of synaptic stimulation
source: We also observed that the extent of eIPSC suppression correlated inversely with the frequency of synaptic stimulation, and that this was most pronounced in the absence of antagonists (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H demonstrating the relationship between stimulation frequency and suppression.

claim: MOR and DOR suppress output from overlapping populations of PV-BC presynaptic terminals
source: Together, these results suggest that MOR and DOR suppress output from overlapping populations of PV-BC presynaptic terminals, and that this suppression is dominated by DOR, both in terms of sensitivity to LE and response kinetics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the occlusion data and kinetics measurements.

claim: Presynaptic suppression is dominated by DOR, both in terms of sensitivity to LE and response kinetics
source: Together, these results suggest that MOR and DOR suppress output from overlapping populations of PV-BC presynaptic terminals, and that this suppression is dominated by DOR, both in terms of sensitivity to LE and response kinetics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the potency and kinetics data showing DOR has greater sensitivity and faster kinetics.

claim: DAMGO caused an ~30% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by one AP (27.27%)
source: Individually, DAMGO and SNC162 both caused an ~30% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by either stimulation protocol (DAMGO 27.27% for one AP, 17.73% for five APs, SNC162 31.18% for one AP, 26.55% for five APs).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient suppression.

claim: DAMGO caused an ~18% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by five APs (17.73%)
source: Individually, DAMGO and SNC162 both caused an ~30% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by either stimulation protocol (DAMGO 27.27% for one AP, 17.73% for five APs, SNC162 31.18% for one AP, 26.55% for five APs).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient suppression.

claim: SNC162 caused an ~31% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by one AP (31.18%)
source: Individually, DAMGO and SNC162 both caused an ~30% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by either stimulation protocol (DAMGO 27.27% for one AP, 17.73% for five APs, SNC162 31.18% for one AP, 26.55% for five APs).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient suppression.

claim: SNC162 caused an ~27% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by five APs (26.55%)
source: Individually, DAMGO and SNC162 both caused an ~30% reduction in the peak ΔG/Gsat evoked by either stimulation protocol (DAMGO 27.27% for one AP, 17.73% for five APs, SNC162 31.18% for one AP, 26.55% for five APs).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient suppression.

claim: When DAMGO and SNC162 were applied together, presynaptic Ca2+ transients were suppressed by ~40%, on average
source: When DAMGO and SNC162 were applied together, these presynaptic Ca2+ transients were suppressed by ~40%, on average (DAMGO then SNC162 40.95% for one AP, 38.92% for five APs, SNC162 then DAMGO 46.08% for one AP, 40.85% for five APs) (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of calcium transient suppression with both drugs.

claim: A 30% reduction in presynaptic Ca2+ is consistent with the strong suppression of PV-BC IPSCs by MORs and DORs
source: Given the nonlinear Ca2+ dependence of vesicular fusion, a 30% reduction in presynaptic Ca2+ is consistent with the strong suppression of PV-BC IPSCs by MORs and DORs (Wu and Saggau, 1997).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established knowledge about the nonlinear relationship between calcium and vesicular fusion, supported by citation.

claim: The marginal effect of adding a second drug suggests convergence on the same pool of VSCCs
source: Furthermore, the marginal effect of adding a second drug suggests convergence on the same pool of VSCCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that combined drug application produces only slightly more suppression than either drug alone.

claim: The inhibition of VSCCs by both MORs and DORs is the most likely mechanism accounting for their effects on inhibitory transmission
source: These results indicate that the inhibition of VSCCs by both MORs and DORs is the most likely mechanism accounting for their effects on inhibitory transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the calcium imaging data showing suppression of presynaptic calcium transients.

claim: Blocking MORs with CTOP had no measurable effect on the light-evoked current (ACSF: 81.7 ± 9.6 pA, n = 9 cells; CTOP: 82.5 ± 12.8 pA, n = 10 cells; not significant)
source: Surprisingly, blocking MORs with CTOP had no measurable effect on the light-evoked current (ACSF: 81.7 ± 9.6 pA, n = 9 cells; CTOP: 82.5 ± 12.8 pA, n = 10 cells; not significant).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of outward currents with statistical comparison.

claim: Blocking DOR with TIPP-Psi greatly reduced the current amplitude (TIPP-Psi: 26.4 ± 4.8 pA, n = 11 cells; p = 0.016)
source: In contrast, blocking DOR with TIPP-Psi greatly reduced the current amplitude (TIPP-Psi: 26.4 ± 4.8 pA, n = 11 cells; p = 0.016), and addition of both drugs completely abolished it (CTOP + TIPP-Psi: 7.1 ± 0.09 pA, n = 5 cells; p = 0.0009; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of outward currents with statistical significance testing.

claim: Addition of both CTOP and TIPP-Psi completely abolished the light-evoked current (CTOP + TIPP-Psi: 7.1 ± 0.09 pA, n = 5 cells; p = 0.0009)
source: In contrast, blocking DOR with TIPP-Psi greatly reduced the current amplitude (TIPP-Psi: 26.4 ± 4.8 pA, n = 11 cells; p = 0.016), and addition of both drugs completely abolished it (CTOP + TIPP-Psi: 7.1 ± 0.09 pA, n = 5 cells; p = 0.0009; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of outward currents with statistical significance testing.

claim: LE exhibited greater potency at DORs than MORs in generating outward currents (EC50 values: ACSF 17.55 ± 2.98 mW, CTOP 7.59 ± 1.26 mW, TIPP-Psi 28.03 ± 7.14 mW)
source: Similar to our observations with presynaptic receptors, LE exhibited greater potency at DORs than MORs in generating outward currents (EC50 values of ACSF: 17.55 ± 2.98 mW, CTOP: 7.59 ± 1.26 mW, TIPP-Psi: 28.03 ± 7.14 mW) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by EC50 values derived from power-response curves.

claim: Somato-dendritic MOR currents in CA1 PV-BCs activated threefold more slowly than DOR-mediated currents (ACSF: 275.9 ± 35.7 ms, n = 11 cells; CTOP: 395.3 ± 109.6 ms, n = 6 cells; TIPP-Psi: 844.1 ± 105.2 ms, n = 9 cells; p = 0.019)
source: Assessment of current activation kinetics with CYLE (6 µM) revealed that, whereas DOR-mediated currents activated with kinetics similar to the MOR currents previously observed in LC neurons, somato-dendritic MOR currents in CA1 PV-BCs activated threefold more slowly, similar to the rate observed for presynaptic MOR in these neurons (ACSF: 275.9 ± 35.7 ms, n = 11 cells; CTOP: 395.3 ± 109.6 ms, n = 6 cells; TIPP-Psi: 844.1 ± 105.2 ms, n = 9 cells; p = 0.019, Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn's multiple comparisons) (Figure 4F and G; Ingram et al., 1997; Banghart and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by time constant measurements with statistical testing and comparison to prior literature.

claim: The small MOR-mediated currents, coupled with similarly slow signaling kinetics in both the presynaptic and somato-dendritic compartments, suggest that MOR signaling is relatively inefficient in CA1 PV-BCs
source: The small MOR-mediated currents, coupled with similarly slow signaling kinetics in both the presynaptic and somato-dendritic compartments, suggest that MOR signaling is relatively inefficient in CA1 PV-BCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed small current amplitudes and slow kinetics.

claim: Ba2+ blocked the majority, but not all, of the current mediated by both MOR and DOR to the same extent (Ba2+ in ACSF: 67.9% ± 4.9%, n = 8 cells; Ba2+ in CTOP: 59.6% ± 9.7%, n = 10 cells; Ba2+ in TIPP-Psi: 67.7% ± 9.1%, n = 11 cells; no significant differences)
source: Consistent with a primary role of GIRK channels, Ba2+ blocked the majority, but notably not all, of the current mediated by both MOR and DOR to the same extent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B) (Ba2+ in ACSF: 67.9% ± 4.9%, n = 8 cells; Ba2+ in CTOP: 59.6% ± 9.7%, n = 10 cells; Ba2+ in TIPP-Psi: 67.7% ± 9.1%, n = 11 cells; no significant differences, ordinary one-way ANOVA).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of current suppression by Ba2+ with statistical analysis.

claim: Inclusion of ZD7288 did not further block the DOR-mediated current (Ba2+, ZD7288 in CTOP: 74.0% ± 5.6%, n = 9 cells; no significant difference)
source: At DORs, inclusion of the HCN channel blocker ZD7288 (1 µM) did not further block the current, suggesting the involvement of additional ion channels (Ba2+, ZD7288 in CTOP: 74.0% ± 5.6%, n = 9 cells; no significant difference, unpaired t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements with statistical testing showing no additional effect of ZD7288.

claim: hMOR overexpression enhanced both the magnitude (57.5 ± 7.8 pA, n = 8 cells, p < 0.0001) and the kinetics (421.8 ± 68.7 ms, n = 8 cells, p = 0.0052) of the MOR-mediated current
source: As predicted, hMOR overexpression enhanced both the magnitude (57.5 ± 7.8 pA, n = 8 cells, p < 0.0001, unpaired t-test) and the kinetics (421.8 ± 68.7 ms, n = 8 cells, p = 0.0052, unpaired t-test) of the MOR-mediated current evoked with a strong light flash in comparison to those recorded from PvalbCre/Rosa26-lsl-tdTomato mice (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing MOR-overexpressing cells to control cells with statistical testing.

claim: Both MOR current amplitude and kinetics correlated strongly with mCherry fluorescence (peak: r = 0.8314, tau on: r = –0.8538)
source: Both parameters correlated strongly with mCherry fluorescence as an indicator of expression level (peak: r = 0.8314, tau on: r = –0.8538, Pearson's correlation coefficient) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between fluorescence and functional measurements.

claim: Low MOR expression levels can account for the surprisingly modest effects of MOR activation in the somato-dendritic compartment of PV-BCs
source: These results indicate that low MOR expression levels can account for the surprisingly modest effects of MOR activation in the somato-dendritic compartment of PV-BCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that increasing MOR expression enhances both current amplitude and kinetics.

claim: Prolonged exposure to DAMGO (1 µM) caused desensitization of the resulting outward current
source: We first confirmed that prolonged exposure to DAMGO (1 µM) caused desensitization of the resulting outward current (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A demonstrating current desensitization over time.

claim: Neither the efficacy nor potency of LE at DORs was affected by MOR desensitization (EC50 in DAMGO: 5.12 ± 0.38 mW, n = 9 cells; CTOP: 6.00 ± 0.42 mW, n = 7 cells)
source: Indicative of a lack of heterologous desensitization, neither the efficacy nor potency of LE at DORs was affected by MOR desensitization (EC50 value of LE in the presence of DAMGO: 5.12 ± 0.38 mW, n = 9 cells; CTOP: 6.00 ± 0.42 mW, n = 7 cells) (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of EC50 values between MOR-desensitized and control conditions.

claim: Prolonged exposure to deltorphin II (1 µM) caused desensitization of the outward current
source: Similarly, prolonged exposure to deltorphin II (1 µM) caused desensitization of the outward current (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E demonstrating current desensitization over time.

claim: Desensitization of DORs using deltorphin II did not affect the ability of LE to elicit somato-dendritic outward currents (EC50 in Delt II: 13.47 ± 1.10 mW, n = 7 cells; TIPP-Psi: 13.47 ± 1.10 mW, n = 11 cells)
source: Desensitization of DORs using deltorphin II did not affect the ability of LE to elicit somato-dendritic outward currents compared to naïve slices bathed in the DOR antagonist TIPP-Psi (EC50 value of LE in the presence of Delt II: 13.47 ± 1.10 mW, n = 7 cells; TIPP-Psi: 13.47 ± 1.10 mW, n = 11 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of EC50 values between DOR-desensitized and control conditions.

claim: MORs and DORs do not undergo heterologous desensitization in CA1 PV-BCs
source: These results reveal that MORs and DORs do not undergo heterologous desensitization in CA1 PV-BCs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the lack of effect of desensitizing one receptor on the function of the other.

claim: TIPP-Psi did not alter the kinetics of the response to DAMGO photorelease in somato-dendritic currents (CNV-Y-DAMGO: 917.6 ± 75.7 ms, n = 11 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 808.8 ± 46.5 ms, n = 7 cells; no significant difference)
source: In both cases, TIPP-Psi did not alter either the kinetics of the response to DAMGO photorelease (GIRK tau on CNV-Y-DAMGO: 917.6 ± 75.7 ms, n = 11 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 808.8 ± 46.5 ms, n = 7 cells; no significant difference, Mann-Whitney test; eIPSC tau on CNV-Y-DAMGO: 476.4 ± 36.9 ms, n = 8 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 441.6 ± 28.1 ms, n = 7 cells; no significant difference, Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 6C and H), its maximal effect (Figure 6D and I), or its power dependence (EC50 values for GIRKs in CNV-Y-DAMGO: 6.86 ± 0.68 mW, n = 8 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 8.53 ± 0.64 mW, n = 7 cells; EC50 values for eIPSCs in CNV-Y-DAMGO: 2.79 ± 0.44 mW, n = 9 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 3.06 ± 0.38 mW, n = 9 cells) (Figure 6E and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by time constant measurements with statistical testing showing no significant difference.

claim: TIPP-Psi did not alter the kinetics of the response to DAMGO photorelease in eIPSCs (CNV-Y-DAMGO: 476.4 ± 36.9 ms, n = 8 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 441.6 ± 28.1 ms, n = 7 cells; no significant difference)
source: In both cases, TIPP-Psi did not alter either the kinetics of the response to DAMGO photorelease (GIRK tau on CNV-Y-DAMGO: 917.6 ± 75.7 ms, n = 11 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 808.8 ± 46.5 ms, n = 7 cells; no significant difference, Mann-Whitney test; eIPSC tau on CNV-Y-DAMGO: 476.4 ± 36.9 ms, n = 8 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 441.6 ± 28.1 ms, n = 7 cells; no significant difference, Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 6C and H), its maximal effect (Figure 6D and I), or its power dependence (EC50 values for GIRKs in CNV-Y-DAMGO: 6.86 ± 0.68 mW, n = 8 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 8.53 ± 0.64 mW, n = 7 cells; EC50 values for eIPSCs in CNV-Y-DAMGO: 2.79 ± 0.44 mW, n = 9 cells; CNV-Y-DAMGO+ TIPP-Psi: 3.06 ± 0.38 mW, n = 9 cells) (Figure 6E and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by time constant measurements with statistical testing showing no significant difference.

claim: TIPP-Psi did not alter the maximal effect of DAMGO photorelease

claim: MORs and DORs are the primary target of widely used opiate analgesics
source: Mu and delta opioid receptors (MORs and DORs) are both Gαi/o-coupled GPCRs that are activated by endogenous opioid neuropeptides such as enkephalin to suppress neuronal excitability and synaptic output. MORs are the primary target of widely used opiate analgesics (e.g. morphine, fentanyl) that are plagued by tolerance, high potential for addiction, and a propensity to cause respiratory depression.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about opioid receptors and their role as targets for analgesics.
